title: Whitman v. American Trucking Associations, Inc. (2001)
shortTitle: Whitman v. American Trucking Associations, Inc. (2001)
summary: Clean Air Act § 109(b) unambiguously bars EPA from considering implementation costs when setting national ambient air quality standards; the instruction to set standards “requisite” to protect public health with an adequate margin of safety is an intelligible principle, and an agency cannot cure an unconstitutional delegation by limiting its own discretion.
notes: Scalia wrote for a unanimous Court on the cost question; Thomas concurred (questioning the intelligible-principle test itself), Stevens concurred in part (joined by Souter, arguing the delegated power is legislative but permissible), and Breyer concurred in part on the cost question. The opinion also contains the well-known line that Congress 'does not, one might say, hide elephants in mouseholes.'

sections.Parties: Christine Todd Whitman, Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, and the EPA represented the federal government; the challenged standards were issued in 1997, before she took office. American Trucking Associations and other companies and organizations, together with Michigan, Ohio and West Virginia, challenged the standards, arguing that EPA’s reading gave it excessive discretion and that the statute should let it weigh compliance costs. The government’s petition (No. 99-1257) and the challengers’ cross-petition (No. 99-1426) were decided together.
sections.Material Facts: Under § 108 of the Clean Air Act EPA identifies covered pollutants and issues air quality criteria; under § 109 it sets national ambient air quality standards which states implement through plans under § 110. Section 109(b)(1) requires primary standards that, in the Administrator’s judgment, based on the criteria and allowing an adequate margin of safety, are requisite to protect public health. On July 18, 1997 EPA revised the ozone and particulate-matter standards, moving ozone from a one-hour to an eight-hour measure without considering compliance costs. A second dispute concerned implementation: Subpart 1 of Part D states general requirements for nonattainment areas, while Subpart 2, added in 1990, classifies ozone areas by severity. In the rule’s preamble EPA announced that it would implement the new standard under Subpart 1, keeping Subpart 2 for the old standard only until an area attained it.
sections.Procedural History: The challengers sought direct review in the D.C. Circuit under § 307(b)(1), 42 U.S.C. § 7607(b)(1), review of rulemaking rather than an appeal from a trial. The panel, 175 F.3d 1027 (1999), with a further decision on rehearing at 195 F.3d 4, held that EPA had construed § 109 to confer discretion without an intelligible principle but, instead of invalidating the statute, remanded so EPA could adopt a limiting construction; Judge Tatel dissented on that point. The panel unanimously rejected consideration of costs, recognized EPA’s power to revise the ozone standard, held that Subpart 2 constrained implementation of a revised standard, and on rehearing treated EPA’s implementation interpretation as final agency action. The Supreme Court granted both petitions, heard argument on November 7, 2000, and decided the case on February 27, 2001, affirming in part, reversing in part and remanding.
sections.Issue: Does § 109(b) permit EPA to consider implementation costs when setting the level requisite to protect public health or welfare? If costs are excluded, does the statute supply an intelligible principle, or does it unconstitutionally delegate legislative power, and can an agency cure such a delegation by restricting its own authority? Separately, was EPA’s announced interpretation of the ozone implementation provisions final and ripe for review, and was it a permissible reading of Subparts 1 and 2?
sections.Holding: Justice Scalia wrote the principal opinion; Parts I and IV were unanimous, all but Breyer joined Part II on costs, and all but Stevens and Souter joined Part III on delegation. Section 109(b) unambiguously excludes implementation costs from the setting of national standards, primary and secondary; the Court did not hold costs irrelevant elsewhere in the Act. Section 109(b)(1) supplies an intelligible principle: standards sufficient, but not more than necessary, to protect public health with an adequate margin of safety, and the Constitution does not require Congress to specify a numerical concentration. An agency’s voluntary self-limitation cannot cure a delegation that lacks a constitutionally adequate standard. EPA’s implementation interpretation was final and ripe, but it could not lawfully read the Act to let Subpart 2’s ozone-specific restrictions largely disappear; the agency was left to find a permissible construction on remand.
sections.Reasoning: Section 109(b)(1) directs EPA to determine what is requisite to protect public health on the basis of scientific criteria; nothing in that instruction tells the agency to weigh health against the cost. Elsewhere Congress expressly mentioned costs and economic feasibility and repeatedly revised the Act without adding such language to § 109; a change of that magnitude cannot hide in terms like “judgment” or “adequate margin,” for Congress does not hide elephants in mouseholes. On delegation, under J. W. Hampton a statute must supply an intelligible principle; the D.C. Circuit’s remedy inverted the inquiry, because an agency choosing how much discretion to exercise would itself make the policy decision the doctrine reserves to Congress. Section 109 identified the task, the evidence, the protected interest and the degree of protection, and it fell comfortably within delegations upheld in Touby, unlike the 1935 statutes struck down in Panama Refining and Schechter. The implementation ruling was final because the preamble stated a considered position; under the then-governing Chevron framework the subparts’ interaction was ambiguous, but EPA’s reading would strip Congress’s detailed ozone restrictions of their force.

topics.lrs-s-intelligible-principle: A health-protection standard within a defined pollution program passed the test despite substantial administrative judgment.
topics.lrs-s-agency-self-limitation: An agency cannot cure an unconstitutional delegation by voluntarily choosing limits Congress failed to supply.
topics.lrs-s-avoidance: Avoidance cannot overcome statutory text that unambiguously excludes cost consideration.
topics.lrs-s-delegation-dimensions: The Court connects the permissible amount of discretion to the scope of the power Congress confers.
topics.lrs-s-caa-109: Whitman construes § 109(b)(1) as barring cost consideration and as supplying the intelligible principle.
topics.lrs-s-article-i-vesting: The nondelegation analysis starts from the Article I vesting of all legislative power in Congress.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Thomas joined the opinion but questioned whether the intelligible-principle test fully enforces Article I, suggesting that some decisions may be too important to delegate even with a principle. Justice Stevens, joined by Justice Souter, agreed the statute was constitutional but would call the delegated power legislative and hold that Congress may delegate it within adequate limits. Justice Breyer agreed costs were excluded here because the Act’s technology-forcing design, structure and history showed it, but would not read regulatory silence generally as forbidding attention to serious adverse consequences. Loper Bright (2024) later overruled Chevron but preserved stare decisis for prior holdings on specific agency actions.
